steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn died in the middle of the night.

Edwin Hart woke to the kind of silence that had weight, the kind that pressed against his eardrums and made the small room at the top of the lighthouse feel suddenly too large. For a brief, confused moment he lay still, tasting salt on the back of his throat, hearing only his own breathing and the distant hiss of waves clawing at the rocks below.

Then it struck him—no groan, no mournful bellow rolling out into the dark. The horn had stopped.

He threw off the blanket and crossed to the narrow window. Outside, the world was a gauze of thick white; the fogbank had come in heavy and fast. Usually, the horn would be sounding steadily by now, warning the fishing boats that hugged this unforgiving coast. And above it all, the lamp would be turning, a steady eye sweeping the horizon.

The lamp burned; that part he had checked before turning in. The horn, though—he listened again, willing it to sound.

Nothing.

In the early days, when the station had first been automated, they’d told him the horn had three redundancies, each checked twice a day by systems ashore. “You’re a caretaker now, Mr. Hart,” the engineer had said, clapping him on the shoulder. “The machinery can look after itself.”

But Edwin had been keeping lights for thirty-seven years. He knew that anything built by hands could fail in the teeth of the sea.

He pulled on his sweater and boots, then stepped onto the iron spiral that curled down the tower’s throat. The lighthouse was never truly warm, but tonight the cold felt intimate, threading through the stone as if the fog itself were seeping in.

Halfway down, he paused by the service hatch that opened to the narrow balcony outside. He pushed it open just enough to peer out. The beam swept across the murk in its patient rotation, a pale scythe cutting the fog. The air tasted like wet metal.

No horn.

He closed the hatch and continued down to the equipment room, where the horn’s machinery sat in a metal cabinet humming softly to itself. Indicator lights glowed green. The control panel showed no alarms. According to the instruments, the horn had been sounding dutifully every thirty seconds all night long.

He stepped closer, resting his fingertips on the cool steel. “Lying to me, are you?” he murmured.

In the early morning quiet, his own voice sounded like someone else’s.

He flicked the manual override switch. The panel clicked. Somewhere above, valves should have opened, air should have rushed, and the great bronze throat should have cried out across the water.

The silence came back thicker than fog.

That was when he felt the old fear rise—an irrational, childhood sort of fear that had nothing to do with electronics. It was the knowledge that there were boats out there, men half a mile off who trusted the rhythm of this place more than their own eyes. He had stood once on the cliff after a storm and watched a trawler’s shattered hull being dragged up, the seaweed clinging to its boards like funerary ribbons.

He took a breath, held it, then exhaled. “All right,” he said. “We do it the hard way.”

He crossed to the locker in the corner and pulled it open. It contained relics from before the automation—oilskins, a coiled rope, an old hand-crank siren. The siren was a dented, ugly thing, its red paint faded to rose. It hadn’t been tested in years; no one had asked him to keep it functional. Still, he had oiled its gears every winter out of habit, the way some men tend plants long after their garden has turned to gravel.

He hauled it out and set it by the narrow door that led to the outer platform below the lantern room. When he pushed the door open, fog flowed in like breath.

Outside, the wind was a gentle, steady push, not enough to tear anything from his hands but strong enough to make the world feel unstable. The light’s beam passed overhead every ten seconds in a pale, ghostly sweep that briefly turned droplets into diamonds, then slipped away again.

Edwin set the siren down, braced his boots against the slick stone, and began to crank.

The mechanism bit immediately, turning with familiar resistance, and the first strangled wail crept out of the horn. It was pitifully small compared to the great automated foghorn, more a human-sized cry than a leviathan’s bellow, but it was sound cutting into silence, a signal against the blankness.

He cranked harder. The siren’s voice rose, gained timbre, stretched out over the water. He pictured it reaching the fishermen, a rope of vibration they could follow to deeper, safer water.

He fell into a rhythm: twenty seconds of cranking, then a few seconds to catch his breath, then on again. The damp worked its way under his collar. The metal handle bruised his palms. Somewhere below, the unseen sea smashed and sucked at the base of the cliff, indifferent to his effort.

Time slipped its moorings. His arms burned. His breath came loud in his ears. The only clock was the sweeping flash above and the rise and fall of the siren’s call.

Between gusts of sound, he imagined he heard an engine far out in the murk—the thrum of a boat moving cautiously, throttled down, listening.

“Come on, then,” he whispered into the white. “Hear me.”

The wind stole his words and scattered them over the waves.

He thought, as he worked, of his father, who had kept a different light on a different coast, long before computers. “You’ll never own a big piece of the world,” his father had told him once, passing him the brass polish, “but you can keep your one small circle clear.” It had seemed, then, an almost insulting sort of ambition. Now, at sixty-three, he understood it as a mercy.

His muscles trembled. The siren’s tone wobbled, sagged, then steadied as he ground his teeth and forced his arms to keep moving.

Then, through the fog, a new sound: a long, low blast, answering his puny wail. A ship’s horn.

He ceased cranking, heart hammering, and listened. The blast came again, closer this time, cautious but certain. He could picture them—whoever they were—correcting course a few degrees, aligning with the faint, reedy cries that marked danger and refuge in the same breath.

He leaned against the parapet, peering into the gray, but the fog kept its secrets. No hull rose out of the gloom, no mast, no deck lights. Only sound confirmed that the world beyond his tiny platform still existed.

“Good,” he muttered. “Good enough.”

After several answering calls, the ship’s horn grew fainter, then faded entirely as it passed and moved on down the coast. The relief that washed through Edwin was out of proportion to the single vessel. It felt like proof that his stubbornness still had weight in the balance.

He cranked the hand siren again, not as furiously now, just enough to make periodic cries, in case another boat wandered close. The minutes stretched. The sky above brightened slightly, losing its inky core to a lighter, milky gray. Dawn, though no sun could be seen.

Eventually his arms simply refused. The siren’s sound dwindled into a tired moan and died. He let the handle slip from his fingers and stood, chest heaving, tasting rust on his tongue.

Inside, the lighthouse was dim but warmer. He stowed the siren by the door, wiped his hands on a rag, and climbed back to the equipment room. The horn’s panel still blazed green and innocent.

He pulled the main breaker.

The room jolted into a deeper quiet. Now the lie lights were dead; for the first time all night the machinery matched reality. He fetched his logbook from the small desk and wrote in his tight, neat hand:

“0300–0500: Automated foghorn failed during dense fog. Manual acoustic signal provided via auxiliary device. Suspected fault in control relay or external monitoring link. Immediate inspection required.”

He hesitated, then added, on a separate line:

“Recommend review of automation redundancies.”

That was as close to anger as his reports ever came.

By the time he reached the lantern room again, the fog had thinned. From this height, he could finally see a mile or two of restless water, slate-colored under the paling sky. Far to the north, a tiny shape moved—a vessel, already well clear.

He watched it a moment, then turned his attention to the lamp: checked the rotation, cleaned a smear of condensation from the glass, ensured the backup generator’s gauges sat where they should. Simple things, within reach.

Sometimes, on still afternoons when the radio was quiet and the only sound was the chuck and slap of the tide, he wondered what would happen when they decided that keepers were redundant too. When even caretakers were deemed excess.

Standing there, fingers resting lightly on the warm metal of the lamp housing, he felt the question rise again: What am I, if I’m not necessary?

Below, a wave boomed against the rocks, sending spray up past the narrow windows in a brief, glittering sheet. The tower shuddered faintly and then settled back into its long-standing poise.

He touched the glass with the back of his knuckles, as he had done every morning for years, the small, private ritual with no one to witness it. “You’re still here,” he said softly, “and so am I.”

Outside, the light completed another patient revolution, casting its white arc across the waking sea.

Somewhere unseen, a gull cried. A thin line of brightness broke along the eastern horizon. The world, for this moment, was held just inside the circle of his care.

Edwin Hart picked up his logbook again, made a note to telephone the harbor office once the line crackle lessened, and then set a kettle on the stove. The work went on, as quiet and steady as the turning of the lens.

The horn would fail again someday, in some other storm. That was the nature of things built to endure; given enough time, they all faltered. But as long as he had hands to crank and breath to spare, there would be a voice at this cliff’s edge, calling out through the fog for anyone who listened.

It was not a grand purpose, not the sort that made statues and songs.

It was enough.
